questions.stem: Which of these is a population rather than a community?
options: All the plants and animals living in one rock pool
Every living thing found in one patch of rainforest
All the grey kangaroos living in one national park
All the animals living together in one national park
questions.explanation: A population is all the members of one species living in an area, so the grey kangaroos in a park form a population. A community is all the populations of different species living and interacting in the same place, which describes each of the other options. Look for whether the group is a single species or many.

questions.stem: In ecology, what is a quadrat used for?
options: Recording the organisms that touch a line across a site
Measuring the temperature and moisture of the soil
Counting organisms in a small, measured area of ground
Trapping animals so they can be marked and released
questions.explanation: A quadrat is a square frame, often 1 m × 1 m, placed on the ground so that the plants or slow-moving animals inside it can be counted. Recording organisms that touch a line describes a line transect, a different sampling method. Because only a small area is counted, the result is scaled up to estimate the whole population.

questions.stem: A student places five 1 m² quadrats at random in a 200 m² paddock and counts 3, 5, 2, 4 and 6 capeweed plants. What is the best estimate of the number of capeweed plants in the paddock?
questions.explanation: The five quadrats hold 20 plants in 5 m², a mean of 4 plants per square metre, and 4 × 200 = 800 plants. The answer 4000 comes from multiplying the total count by the paddock area without first dividing by the number of quadrats. The answer 4 is the density per square metre, which still has to be scaled up to the whole paddock.

questions.stem: Why should quadrats be placed at random, for example using random-number coordinates, rather than wherever the student chooses?
options: To avoid bias towards spots that look crowded or interesting
To make sure that every organism in the area gets counted
Because random placement gives an exact count of the population
Because random placement means that fewer quadrats are needed
questions.explanation: People tend to put quadrats where plants look thick or unusual, which would make the estimate too high, so random placement keeps the sample representative. Sampling never counts every organism and never gives an exact figure; it gives an estimate. Using more quadrats, not fewer, is what makes the estimate more reliable.

questions.stem: An ecologist wants to see how the plants change from the high-tide line of a beach back to the sand dunes behind it. Which sampling method suits this best?
options: A single quadrat placed in the middle of the dunes
A belt transect running from the shoreline inland
Quadrats placed at random across the whole area
Capture–mark–recapture of plants along the beach
questions.explanation: A transect is a line laid across an environmental gradient, and a belt transect places quadrats along it, so it shows how species change with distance from the sea. Random quadrats are ideal for estimating numbers across a fairly even area, but they do not show a pattern of change along a gradient. Capture–mark–recapture is for animals that move around, not for plants.

questions.stem: Ecologists catch 40 bush rats, mark them and release them. A week later they catch 50 rats, and 10 of these are marked. Using the Lincoln index, what is the estimated population?
questions.explanation: The Lincoln index estimates the population as (number marked × number caught in the second sample) ÷ number of marked animals recaptured, so N = (40 × 50) ÷ 10 = 200. The answer 2000 forgets to divide by the recaptures. The answer 80 simply counts the different rats that were handled, which is always less than the real population.

questions.stem: In a capture–mark–recapture study of frogs, 30 frogs are marked and released. In the second sample, 6 of the frogs caught are marked, and the population is estimated at 150. How many frogs were caught in the second sample?
questions.explanation: Rearranging N = (M × C) ÷ R gives C = (N × R) ÷ M = (150 × 6) ÷ 30 = 30 frogs. The answer 25 comes from 150 ÷ 6, which leaves out the number marked. A quick check: (30 × 30) ÷ 6 = 150, which matches the estimate.

questions.stem: In a capture–mark–recapture study, many of the paint marks wear off before the second sample is caught. How will this affect the population estimate?
options: It will be unaffected, because the total caught has not changed
It will be too low, because marked animals become easier to catch
It will be too high, because fewer marked animals are recognised
It will be too low, because fewer marked animals are recognised
questions.explanation: If marks are lost, the number of recaptures counted (R) is smaller than it should be, and dividing by a smaller number makes N = (M × C) ÷ R too large. Thinking the estimate falls is the common slip; it helps to try numbers, such as dividing 2000 by 5 instead of by 10. This is why the method assumes marks stay on and are not missed.

questions.stem: Which condition must hold for a capture–mark–recapture estimate to be reliable?
options: Marked animals mix randomly back through the population
Marked animals stay close to where they were first released
Only the healthiest animals are caught in the second sample
Many animals migrate in and out between the two samples
questions.explanation: The method assumes the marked animals spread evenly through the population, so the fraction marked in the second sample matches the fraction marked overall. If marked animals stayed near the release point, a second sample taken there would contain too many of them. It also assumes no animals arrive or leave between the samples.

questions.stem: Which pair of factors both increase the size of a population?
options: Births and emigration
Deaths and immigration
Deaths and emigration
Births and immigration
questions.explanation: A population grows when individuals are added by being born or by moving in (immigration). Emigration means individuals moving out, so it lowers the population, as deaths do. The names are easy to confuse: immigrants come in, emigrants exit.

questions.stem: What is the carrying capacity of an environment for a species?
options: The total number of different species the environment can hold
The fastest rate at which the species’ population is able to grow
The number of individuals that move into the environment each year
The largest population of it the environment can support long term
questions.explanation: Carrying capacity is set by limiting factors such as food, water, shelter and space, and a population tends to level off around it. It refers to one species, not to the number of different species in an area. A population can briefly overshoot its carrying capacity, but it cannot stay above it.

questions.stem: Rabbits released onto an island increase slowly at first, then very rapidly, and then their numbers level off. What explains the levelling off?
options: Limiting factors such as food and space now balance births with deaths
The rabbits have stopped breeding because they have all become adults
Every rabbit on the island has become immune to all of its diseases
The island’s carrying capacity keeps rising as the rabbit numbers rise
questions.explanation: This S-shaped (logistic) curve flattens when the population nears the carrying capacity, because competition for food and space raises deaths and lowers births until they are roughly equal. Adult rabbits keep breeding, so ageing is not the cause. Becoming immune to disease would remove a limiting factor and let numbers keep rising rather than level off.

questions.stem: A population graph rises more and more steeply with no sign of slowing down (a J-shaped curve). What does this suggest about the population?
options: The population has reached the carrying capacity of its habitat
Deaths are now greater than births in the population each year
Predators are keeping the size of the population under control
Resources are plentiful and limiting factors are not yet acting
questions.explanation: J-shaped growth happens when there is plenty of food and space, so each generation adds more individuals than the last. A population at carrying capacity would show a flat line, and more deaths than births would make the graph fall. J-shaped growth cannot continue forever, and it often ends in a sudden crash when resources run out.

questions.stem: Mayfly and stonefly nymphs are common in a creek upstream of a farm but almost absent downstream. What does this most likely indicate?
options: The downstream water is cleaner, as these nymphs avoid clean water
The downstream water is colder, which suits these nymphs much better
The downstream water has more food, so the nymphs no longer need it
The downstream water is polluted, as these nymphs need clean water
questions.explanation: Mayfly and stonefly nymphs are indicator species that need clean, oxygen-rich water, so their disappearance suggests pollution, such as fertiliser or sediment running off the farm. Pollution-tolerant animals such as worms and some fly larvae often increase in their place. Lichens are used the same way on land, because many species die where the air is polluted.

questions.stem: Two paddocks each contain the same four plant species and 100 plants in total. Paddock A has 25 plants of each species; paddock B has 85 of one species and 5 of each of the others. Which statement is correct?
options: Paddock B has greater richness because one species dominates
Their evenness is equal, but paddock A has greater richness
Paddock B has greater evenness because one species dominates
Their richness is equal, but paddock A has greater evenness
questions.explanation: Species richness is simply the number of species, which is four in both paddocks. Evenness describes how equally the individuals are shared among those species, and paddock A’s equal split is perfectly even. When one species dominates, as in paddock B, evenness and overall diversity are lower even though richness is the same.
